                              When the excitation is a plane wave, we are generally interested in the echo area
                         or radar cross section (RCS) of the wire structure. The RCS is measured in units of
                         length squared and is given by
                                                                           |Er |2
                                                          σ = lim 4πr 2           .                        (4.61)
                                                               r →∞        |Ei |2
                         If the wire length is measured in wavelengths, then the units of σ are square wave-
                         lengths (λ2o ), and if the wire length is measured in meters then σ will be given in
                         m2 . The RCS of the λ/2, λ, and 3λ long wires are shown in Figures 4-16 and 4-17.
                         The effect of wire thickness on the wire’s RCS is predicted in Figure 4-18, where
                         the value of broadside (θi = 90◦ ) σ is plotted as a function of the wire’s length for
                         three different radii. This is a characteristic curve for the wire scatterer and displays
                         its resonant behavior when 2 ≈ (n + 1)λo /2 for odd n. Basically, the RCS of the
                         wire at those lengths reaches a local peak with each successive peak becoming larger
                         as 2 is increased. This property of the wire has been explored in many practical
                         situations, and we remark that the location of the RCS peaks should correspond to
                         the wire length at which I m(Z in ) ≈ 0.
                              We observe that the echo area pattern of the longer wire as given in Figure 4-17
                         has a very strong lobe near θ = π (near grazing). This is a lobe characteristic to
                         all thin-wire scattering patterns and is always the one closest to θ = 0◦ or θ = π .
                         It is often referred to as the traveling wave lobe, and to explain its presence let
                         us assume that the wire is infinite in length. The incident plane wave (4.47) will
                         then generate a current of the form I1 e jko z cos θi , where I1 is a complex constant
                         proportional to the incident wave’s strength and can be computed analytically. This

                           generates additional reflected currents of the form I2 e jko z and I3 e− jko z , where I2 and
                           I3 are again complex constants. Thus the current on the wire due to a plane wave
                           excitation can be approximately represented as


                                                                                3
                                                                     I (z) =         In e jkn z                  (4.62)
                                                                               n=1




                           with k1 = ko cos θo , k2 = +ko , and k3 = −ko . From this representation it is not
                           difficult to observe from the radiation integral (4.49) that the scattered field would
                           peak at θ = π − θi and at θ = 0 or π if the coefficients In were comparably weighted.
                           However, this is not the case, and it turns out that the traveling wave lobe peak occurs
                           when I2,3 are at maximum.
                                The expansion (4.62) is, of course, a linear sum of three full-wave basis functions,
                           similar to those given by (4.22) through (4.23). It was constructed on the basis of the
                           physical phenomena that take place on the straight wire and is thus most efficient
                           for computational purposes. However, as noted earlier, this expansion (which may
                           be referred to as a solution wave expansion) is specific to the straight wire scatterer
                           and cannot be employed for other wire shapes or arbitrary multiple wire structures.

        These can be evaluated numerically using, for example, Simpson’s, midpoint, or
        Gaussian rules of integration (Abramowitz and Stegun, 1964). Clearly, (4.70) along
        with (4.68) and (4.69) demand that the boundary conditions be satisfied on an
        average sense over the wire subintervals. When the weighting functions are piece-
        wise constant, each current value over the subinterval is given equal weighting in
        this averaging process. A variety of other choices for Wm (z) have, though, been
        employed successfully in the past. When Wm (z) are chosen to be the same as the
        current expansion basis function, the procedure for deriving the resulting system of
        equations is referred to as Galerkin’s method (Jones, 1956; Kantorovich and Krylov,
        1959). We also note that when

                                              Wm (z) = δ(z − z m )                                     (4.76)

        (4.70) reduces to the system (4.30) derived by the point-matching technique. The
        previous procedure for discretizing the integral equation is formally referred to as the
        weighted residual method but is most often called the method of moments (MoM)1 .
        Also, the pulse-basis–point-matching procedure is more formally referred to as the
        collocation method.
             The application of Galerkin’s technique has been studied extensively and has
        been found quite robust for many applications. It is indeed pleasing to know that the
        method minimizes the residual in the least squares sense. It can be expected that the
        Galerkin’s implementation leads to more robust and efficient computer codes. For
        example, in the case of a pulse-basis expansion, the Galerkin’s solution converges to
        the correct current using 30% to 50% fewer segments as shown in Figure 4-19. The
        solution convergence improves even further if higher-order basis functions are used
        and next we describe the Galerkin’s formulation and derive the resulting system of
        equations for the subsectional sinusoidal basis.

                            4.8            METHOD OF MOMENTS FOR NONLINEAR
                         WIRES
                         Typically, the antenna or scatterer will be composed of curved wire elements. Also,
                         it is possible to model continuous metallic surfaces with a wire grid of sufficient
                         density as shown in Figure 4-26. Acceptable grid densities are often 10 or more
                         wires per linear wavelength on the surface.
                              To develop a method of moments formulation applicable to curved wires, let us
                         consider the following curved wire geometry and assume for simplicity a constant
                         wire thickness equal to 2a  λ. As usual, we are interested in determining the wire

                         of the wire.

          4.11 ITERATIVE SOLUTION METHODS:
        THE CONJUGATE GRADIENT METHOD
        Instead of inverting the impedance matrix [Z mn ] for a solution of the system (4.33)
        or (4.73), one could employ an iterative solution scheme. Among the numerous
        iterative solution schemes for such a system, the conjugate gradient (CG) method is
        most attractive because it guarantees convergence in a maximum of N iterations for
        an N -dimensional system (ignoring round-off errors). The CG method is a nonlinear,
        semidirect iterative scheme and was introduced by Hesteness and Steifel (1952)
        independently more than 40 years ago. Beginning with a random initial guess of
        the solution (including the zero) vector {In }, convergence is accomplished via a
        systematic orthogonalization of the solution vector with respect to the residual vector
        defined as the difference between the left- and right-hand sides of the system. The
        residual vector is computed at the end of each iteration and is used to find the next
        correction to the solution vector. The correction vectors are chosen to be orthogonal to
        the residual vectors, which are linearly independent. This is an essential condition for
        guaranteeing the convergence of the algorithm since at the N th iteration the solution
        vector would have been constructed by N independent vectors (conjugate directions)
        which form a basis set of the N-dimensional space. Moreover, the algorithm will
        first proceed with corrections that will most greatly impact the minimization of the
        next residual vector. Consequently, convergence to within a reasonable degree of
        accuracy can be achieved after only a few (normally less than N /3) iterations.
              The CG algorithm for the pertinent system proceeds as follows (Volakis et al.,
        1998; Wilton and Wheeler, 1991):
              Initialize the residual vector and conjugate direction:

        The wire structure considered in the previous chapter is perhaps the simplest version
        of a three-dimensional geometry because it can be modeled by a filamentary current.
        In the case of other antenna structures such as reflectors, horns, or microstrip patches,
        the current will be a three-dimensional function, and this leads to more involved
        kernels for the resulting integral equations. The complexity of the integral equation
        is increased further when we consider the radar scattering by an aircraft structure,
        a portion of which may be nonmetallic or coated with a dielectric. Thus, before
        proceeding with the treatment of three-dimensional structures, it is instructive to
        consider solutions of simpler structures that can serve to understand and validate the
        methods. It turns out that, in the case of scattering, we can obtain information from
        two-dimensional treatments, which under certain assumptions can be extrapolated
        to three dimensions.
             In this chapter we consider the numerical solution of the scattering by (a) a
        flat and a curved resistive strip, (b) a dielectric strip, (c) a homogeneous dielectric
        cylinder, and (d) an inhomogeneous dielectric cylinder.

             It is seen that (5.26) displays the familiar behavior of the current density near
        the edge of the strip as discussed   √ already. That is, near the edges, the current of
        the metallic strips grows as 1/ d, where d is a measure of the distance from the
        edge. Equation (5.26) obviously states that the current density goes to infinity at
        the edge of the strip, implying that the magnetic field must also be infinite at the
        edge. One should therefore question its physical meaning and significance since in
        practice we cannot expect such behavior. To explain the validity of the result, we
        should note that any physical requirement should be imposed on the energy carried
        by the field. Thus, we can demand only that the power is finite at the edge, and in
        this particular case it can be shown that the power propagating away from the edge is
        indeed finite. Moreover, in practice the strip will have a finite conductivity, in which
        case it must be modeled as a resistive strip.

        5.1.2.1 Pulse-Basis–Point-Matching Solution
        The solution of (5.30) using pulse-basis expansion and point matching is not gen-
        erally a suitable approach because of the kernel’s singularity, which is of order R −2
        as R → 0. Consequently, the resulting integral is improper unless at least one of
        the derivatives is transferred to the current. Nevertheless, such a solution can be
        meaningful if we retain the second derivative outside the integrand and then carry
        out the differentiation after the integration is completed. In this manner all integrals
        remain proper and can be evaluated in the usual manner.

        and provided, of course, the chosen interval is sufficiently small to accurately rep-
        resent the current distribution. In contrast to E-polarization, for H -polarization the
        near-diagonal matrix elements do not diminish as rapidly, and this is attributed to
        the presence of H1(2) , which is more singular than Ho(2) . Consequently, the condition
        of the H -polarization impedance matrix is generally much larger (compared with

                  5.2                                               METALLIC CYLINDERS
        The geometry of the cylinder is shown in Figure 5-15 and we shall assume that the
        cylinder’s boundary C is of arbitrary shape. The pertinent integral equations for the
        equivalent surface currents are given by (3.98), and we note that the TM (or E-
        polarization) equation was already employed in Section 5.1.1. In that case, the TM
        integral equation was enforced on a flat strip to yield the surface current Jz (x). Here
        we must discretize (3.98a) for an arbitrary curved surface where ρ and ρ  will now
        be functions of both x and y. Thus, in performing the required integrations over the
        contour C, it will be necessary to employ some suitable parametric representation
        for the contour line. The same must, of course, be done for the TE integral equation
        (3.98b) whose implementation is more challenging because of the kernel’s higher

                              As noted earlier, the transverse magnetic (TM) integral equation (5.70) is valid
                         for open as well as closed metallic surfaces and can thus be used to study the effect
                         of curvature on the scattering cross section (echowidth) of a metallic strip. To do
                         so, we consider the five circular strips curved as illustrated in Figure 5-19a, but all
                         have the same circumference of 2λo . The curvature (κ = 1/a, where a is the strip
                         radius) of the strips varies from 0 to π/λo and the one with the highest curvature is
                         actually a circular cylinder of radius λo /π. The bistatic echowidths for each of the
                         strips with φ = φo = 90◦ is given in Figure 5-19b. It is seen that the echowidth of
                         each strip peaks at the backscatter and forward directions regardless of the strip’s
                         curvature. Also, at these locations, the echowidth is larger for the flatter strips and,
                         in fact, at backscatter (φ = 90◦ ) it is equal to ko w = 8π λo for the flat strip and
                         closer to πa = π/κ for the curved strips. The last result is based on a geometrical

        which is precisely the result in (5.91). This alternative procedure simply points out
        that the self-cell element can be evaluated without a need to invoke Cauchy’s principal
        value theorem. Instead, by retaining the derivative outside the integral, the integration
        can be carried out in the standard manner. The appropriate differentiation can then
        be performed on the integrated quantity. In other words, the integral equation is
        enforced at a point just off the boundary surface, thus avoiding the improper integral
        altogether. The testing point is then moved onto the surface upon completion of the
        required integration and differentiations.

            5.3 H-POLARIZED (TE) SCATTERING
        BY CURVED RESISTIVE STRIPS
        As discussed in Section 3.2.3, the magnetic field integral equation (MFIE) (5.80),
        by its derivation, is suitable only for modeling closed boundaries such as those of
        metallic cylinders. When modeling resistive strips, flat or curved (see Figure 5-20),
        it is necessary to employ the EFIE given in (3.99), which reduces to (5.30) when
        generalized to treat flat resistive strips. In the case of curved resistive strips, (3.99)

                                  An application of resistive sheets is the simulation of dielectric layers as dis-
                            cussed in Section 1.12. The idea of approximating a thin dielectric layer by a resistive
                            sheet can be generalized to model thick dielectric cylinders. Specifically, the cylinder
                            is first decomposed into stacks or an arrangement of dielectric layers as illustrated,
                            for example, in Figure 5-21. Each dielectric layer or shell is then replaced by a sheet
                            of resistivity Re Z o = − j Z o /[ko τ ( r − 1)], where τ denotes the shell-layer thick-
                            ness, and r is the corresponding relative dielectric constant (which can be a function
                            of ρ). The backscatter echowidths of a rectangular 1λo × 0.4λo dielectric cylinder
                            and a thin circular dielectric shell using the proposed sheet simulation are given in

        Figure 5-22. It is seen that the sheet simulation yields quite accurate results when
        compared with a more rigorous formulation (see Richmond, 1965) which will be
        discussed later. However, one should recognize that such sheet simulations are not
        always as accurate, and furthermore the model’s accuracy depends on the particular
        arrangement of the layers. For example, were we to model the rectangular dielec-
        tric block in Figure 5-21 using five planar dielectric layers (rather than rectangular
        shells), the computed echowidth on the basis of this sheet model will not be as ac-
        curate for small φ angles. This is because the sheet model composed of parallel flat
        layers neglects altogether the presence of the y-directed polarization currents, which
        are most important for incidences close to the x-axis. The importance of the vertical
        polarization currents is illustrated in Figure 5-23 where we consider the scattering
        by a 0.1λo thick dielectric layer.
             Another example calculation that cannot be done with the MFIE is shown in
        Figure 5-24. This figure shows the backscatter echowidth of an ogive cylinder with
        a strip attached to its left. The total length of the cylinder is 10λo , and about 110
        segments were used for its numerical simulation. It is seen that the pulse-basis–point-
        matching solution is in good agreement with a solution based on the volume-surface
        integral equation (VSIE) given by (3.114) and whose solution is discussed later. As
        expected, the echowidth is higher around the broadside angular region and drops to
        low values near grazing.

                             5.4 PIECEWISE HOMOGENEOUS
                         DIELECTRIC CYLINDERS

                  5.5      ELIMINATION OF INTERIOR RESONANCES
        As discussed in Section 3.1.5, the electric field integral equations (EFIE) and mag-
        netic field integral equations (MFIE), whether applied to two-dimensional or three-
        dimensional problems, are prone to yielding erroneous results at certain frequencies.
        Failure of a certain integral equation solution to yield accurate results is manifested
        in the form of an ill-conditioned system (a matrix system with a condition number
        of 107 or greater is usually considered as ill-conditioned). This occurs only when
        the boundary integral equations are enforced on closed-boundary contours as was
        the case of metallic and dielectric cylinders considered in Sections 5.2 and 5.4. The
        EFIE integral equations applied to planar and curved strips (not forming a closed
        surface) do not suffer from such failures, which can be identified to occur at and near
        the resonant frequencies of the cavity/waveguide formed by the closed boundary. To
        appreciate the severity of the problem, the reader is referred to Figure 5-28 (Collins,
        Jin, and Volakis, 1992) which displays the TM backscatter echowidth of the metallic
        circular cylinder as a function of frequency obtained from a solution of the MFIE
        given in Section 5.2.1. It is seen that the MFIE solution is replete with “spikes”
        that occur precisely at the resonant frequencies of the circular cylinder marked for
        reference by the vertical bars along the frequency axis. The spikes are obviously
        nonphysical and uncharacteristic of the exact series solution given in Section 5.2.1
        and plotted for reference in Figure 5-28a. As expected, at the resonant frequencies
        the value of the computed scattered field on the surface of the circular cylinder
        via the MFIE is also in error when compared with the exact series solution (see
        Figure 5-28b).
             In Section 3.1.5 we presented the combined field integral equation (CFIE) for-
        mulation as a means of overcoming the inherent failure of the EFIE and MFIE
        solutions. This technique is one of the most popular remedies to the problem and has
        been discussed extensively in the literature (Mautz and Harrington, 1978; Govind
        and Wilton, 1979; Peterson, 1990; Putnam and Medgyesi-Mitchang, 1991). Here we

                              We remark that the combined field formulation is only one method in overcoming
                         the non-uniqueness of the EFIE and MFIE when applied to closed boundaries.
                         Alternative approaches have been considered including the overspecification of the
                         boundary conditions (Yaghjian, 1981; Mittra and Klein, 1975) and the combination
                         of electric and magnetic currents (Mautz and Harrington, 1979), the latter being
                         useful in radiation problems. Recently, a rather interesting technique based on the
                         “complexification” of the wave number was introduced (Collins, Jin, and Volakis,
                         1992). In accordance with this method, no new integral equation needs to be derived.
                         Instead, it requires only that the wave number in the MFIE or EFIE be replaced by
                         αko , where α is a complex constant with a very small imaginary part. It has been
                         shown that the interior resonances of the EFIE, MFIE, or any other boundary integral
                         equation are eliminated by simply set α equal to 1 − j0.001 up to 1 − j0.005. The
                         success of this approach is indeed a consequence of the uniqueness theorem.


                             5.6 SIMULATION OF INHOMOGENEOUS
                         DIELECTRIC CYLINDERS
                         The aforementioned boundary integral formulations are suitable for homogeneous
                         and piecewise homogeneous dielectric cylinders. Natural material (e.g., soil, vege-
                         tation, human tissue, or even man-made composites) are typically inhomogeneous.
                         Consequently, we cannot break up the computational domain in separate homoge-
                         neous sections for analysis, as was illustrated in Figure 3-5. To solve for the fields
                         scattered by or in the presence of an inhomogeneous structure, it is necessary to
                         consider the volume and volume-surface integral equations discussed in Section
                         3.2.5. In this section we first present the solution of the traditional volume integral
                         equation before proceeding with the solution of the more efficient volume-surface
                         integral equation given in (3.114).

                         5.6.1 Volume Integral Equation

        to evaluate Amn and Amn . The circular cell approximation is based on the equal
        area concept and therefore offers a way of modeling the contribution of small non-
        rectangular or other shape elements that remain after the subdivision of the cylinder.
        No special treatment of these elements √      is required other than the introduction of
        a circular cylinder of radius a = A/π , where A is the area of the original
        non-rectangular element.
             In solving the system (5.131) it is advisable to normalize each of the rows
        by the largest entry of that row to improve the matrix condition number before
        inversion. Also, to avoid large matrix element values when r or μ R are near unity,
        we can instead solve for the field quantities E zn = jko YoJ(zn r −1) , Hxn = jko ZMo (μ
                                                                                               xn

                    M yn
        Hyn = jko Z o (μr −1) , which, of course, remain bounded throughout the dielectric.
             Once the system (5.131) is solved, the far-zone scattered field can be evaluated
        from (2.133). It should be noted, however, that for better accuracy and consistency
        the cell integrations should be over the same cross sectional area used for the eval-
        uation of the matrix elements. That is, if circular elements were used, the far-zone
        integral should also be evaluated by integrating over the sum of the circular do-
        mains defining those elements. Needless to say, since the previously given solution
        applies to dielectric cylinders with nontrivial permeability and permittivity, dual-
        ity can be invoked for the solution of the fields under TE excitation (see (5.28)).
        Some illustrative scattering patterns using Richmond’s formulation were shown in
        Figure 5-22.

        5.6.2 Volume-Surface Integral Equation
        The previously presented solution and in particular that employing circular elements,
        has been found quite accurate for modeling cylinders having nominal values of
        relative dielectric constants (e.g., up to 10). However, for large values of r or μr , it
        is necessary that the discretized geometry maintains as much as possible the shape
        and detail of the original geometry. Given that x and y must be generally selected
        to be less than 0.1λd , where λd is the wavelength in the dielectric, it becomes rather
        difficult to maintain geometrical fidelity for arbitrary cross section cylinders when
        modeling them as a collection of rectangular and circular elements. Moreover, as
        discussed in Section 3.2.4, the previous solution is not as efficient when both r and
        μr are greater than unity.
             To improve upon the geometrical modeling, one could choose to tessellate the
        cylinder’s cross section using triangles or second-order quadrilaterals. The latter
        are four-sided elements whose sides, instead of being flat, are second-order curves.
        Further, to reduce the number of unknown current coefficients, we could instead
        choose to represent the scattered fields directly in terms of the total electric or mag-
        netic fields as given in (3.114). Next we consider the solution of the VSIE (3.114)
Volakis-7200025      book       ISBN : 9781891121937           October 5, 2011       13:52         252




   252                      CHAPTER        5      Two-Dimensional Scattering

                            using isoparametric quadrilaterals (four-sided elements) to tessellate the cylinder’s
                            cross section. The word isoparametric (“iso” is the Greek word for equal) implies
                            elements that have the same order of approximation in representing the fields and
                            the geometry/contour of the dielectric. It is, of course, logical to choose isopara-
                            metric elements because, as can be expected, a quadratic field expansion cannot
                            improve the solution accuracy when we insist on using square rectangular elements
                            for discretizing a dielectric scatterer having circular or other nonlinear contours. The
                            second-order (meaning the sides are quadratic curves) quadrilateral, to be employed
                            in the subsequent integral equation solution, is illustrated in Figure 5-35. The con-
                            tour of the cylinder will be modeled using quadratic line segments that are depicted
                            in Figure 5-36. An example of such a tessellation applied to a circular cylinder is
                            illustrated in Figure 5-37.
                                 A characteristic of each geometric element (line, area, or volume) is its shape
                            function. These shape functions allow, for example, a curved line segment to be
                            mapped to a straight segment or an arbitrary quadrilateral to be mapped to a square as
                            shown in Figures 5-35 and 5-36. These mappings are necessary to perform the
                            integrations required for evaluating the matrix elements.

                            straight line in the ζ − η plane is given by

             To discretize (5.145) we first tessellate the cylinder’s volume into M quadrilat-
        erals and the contour C into N second-order curvilinear segments as illustrated in
        Figure 5-38. If certain sections of the cylinder are metallic, it is necessary only to
        discretize along the contour enclosing the metal. Further, for TM incidence it is not
        even required to consider the metallic contours because F = E z vanishes on these
        contours. The modeling of exposed metallic boundaries may, in this case, be done
        by considering a thin dielectric layer having r = 1 − j106 and a minimal thickness
        of 0.01λ or so.

        The previous chapters provided the framework for solving integral equations. But so
        far, we have yet to consider scattering or radiation from general three-dimensional
        (3-D) structures. The subject of scattering by 3-D structures using full-wave methods
        was a focus during the 1980s; Rao, Wilton and Glisson’s (1982) classic paper was
        among the first on the subject. Previously, Livesay and Chen (1974) had considered
        volumetric modeling of biological tissues via the method of moments (MoM) so-
        lution of volume integral equations using simple cubic elements. Surface integral
        equation formulations for homogeneous material bodies were developed by Putnam
        and Medgyesi-Mitchang (1991). Later, parametric elements were introduced for
        both curvilinear volumetric modeling (Graglia, 1988) and for accurate modeling of
        curved surfaces (Song and Chew, 1995). Better geometry modeling of conformal el-
        ements were complemented by higher-order basis functions (BFs) (Graglia, Wilton,
        and Peterson, 1997) for much improved MoM accuracy and reduction in compu-
        tational cost. Additionally, surface integral equations were hybridized by the finite
        element methods (Jin and Volakis, 1991; Antilla and Alexopoulos, 1994), result-
        ing in state-of-the-art simulation tools that can efficiently model arbitrary material
        domains as well as conducting regions in real-life problems.
             In this chapter, we summarize the method of moments for surface and volume
        integral equations. In the first half, surface and volume modeling techniques are
        outlined along with the definitions of frequently used flat and curvilinear elements.
        Basis functions and differential operators (gradient, divergence, and curl) are given
        in curvilinear coordinates, and details of the MoM implementation are presented.
        Construction of the MoM matrix, numerical integrations, and careful handling of
        singular integrals are given in detail, as these constitute the main steps in the imple-
        mentation. We conclude by providing volumetric modeling for material regions and
        several numerical examples.

                                     6.1         SCATTERING BY METALLIC BODIES
                              The unique radar return or signature of an airborne or ground vehicle, as seen by
                              the radar, is called the radar cross section (RCS). Consider a representative fighter
                              aircraft, as in Figure 6-1, illuminated by a transmitting radar antenna placed at a
                              substantial distance from the target. The electromagnetic wave that impinges on the
                              target can be approximated by a plane wave. To keep our analysis simple, we will
                              also assume that the aircraft is a metallic surface denoted by S. Thus, for our radar
                              scattering analysis, we may proceed to use the electric field integral equation (EFIE),
                              magnetic field integral equation (MFIE), or the combined field integral equation
                              (CFIE) developed in Chapter 3. This section considers these integral equations as
                              applied to perfectly electrically conducting (PEC) (i.e., metallic) scatterers.


                              6.1.1 Electric, Magnetic, and Combined Field
                              Integral Equations
                              Let us consider the problem of plane wave scattering by an airframe structure as
                              in Figure 6-1. For simplicity, we will assume that this scatterer is PEC. Therefore,
                              our first step in computing the associated RCS is to evaluate the current density
                              J on the surface S of the airframe. This can be done by invoking the EFIE given
                              in (3.42a). For PEC structures, the EFIE is generated by enforcing the boundary
                              condition tˆ · (Ei + Es ) = 0, where tˆ is the unit tangent vector to the body’s surface S
                              (see Figure 6-1). Doing so yields

        6.1.2 Triangular Element Mesh Representations
        A first step in the numerical solution of (6.1) and (6.3) is the discretization of the
        scatterer surface S. This is done by breaking up S as a collection of triangles or
        quadrilaterals (see Figures 6-1 and 6-2), a process referred to as gridding or meshing
        of the surface. It constitutes the first approximation in the numerical solution process.
        A next step is to define a suitable current density representation on each surface
        element.
             Let’s for the moment focus on triangular elements to grid (or mesh) the surface S.
        This is a popular approach for modeling arbitrary structures and is widely used due
        to the availability of gridding software tools for triangular meshes. As depicted in
        Figure 6-2, the geometry is approximated by a collection of flat triangular elements,
        or patches. In electromagnetics, the use of flat triangulations was sparked by the

                              To represent the geometry and induced surface currents we begin by defining
                         each triangular element in terms of its three vertices (ri , r j , rk ) shown in Figure 6-3.
                         These vertices are associated with local and global numbering schemes. The local
                         numbers (for the triangle’s nodes and edges) are conveniently chosen as (1, 2, 3).
                         Correspondingly, the global numbers for the nodes will be denoted as (i, j, k) and
                         are unique in the entire surface grid. As a rule, we choose to denote local edge e p
                         to have the same local number as the node n p located across the edge e p . With this
                         numbering scheme, the local edge 3 of the triangular element connects local nodes 1
                         and 2; local edge 1 connects local nodes 2 and 3, and local edge 2 connects local
                         nodes 3 and 1. This numbering convention also defines the unit vector normal to the
                         triangular element in the right-hand rule sense.
                              The local and global numbering of the nodes and elements provide a convenient
                         way to define the mesh of the scattering surface as an ordered list. For example, con-
                         sider the section of a surface mesh depicted in Figure 6-4. The depicted mesh around
                         triangle 34(t34 ) is defined by the vectors r10 , r55 , and r38 . Likewise, triangle 22 is
                         defined by the three nodes r29 , r55 , and r10 . That is, the local edge 3 of triangle 34
                         coincides with local edge 1 of triangle 22, implying that the same edge in a mesh can
                         be identified in multiple ways. Thus, an interconnectivity relationship (or table) that
                         uniquely identifies all edges and nodes comprising the grid is an essential aspect of
                         integral equation solutions. As part of this process, a node connectivity table and a co-
                         ordinates listing table for each node are generated, as illustrated in Tables 6-1 and 6-2.
                              Given the three nodes defining each triangle, any surface location within the tri-
                         angle can be obtained via the simplex or barycentric coordinates (ζ1 , ζ2 , ζ3 ) (Volakis,

                            6.1.3 Rao–Wilton–Glisson Basis Functions
                            The triangular mesh proposed in Figure 6-4 leads to a restricted set of basis functions

                            and Glisson, 1982) are such that the unknowns {xn } represent the current flowing
                            perpendicular to the edge joining two triangles. Two such triangles are depicted in
                            Figure 6-7 and share the edge defined by the location vectors r j and rk . A key aspect
                            of the RWG basis is that they taper linearly to zero at the nodes opposite to the edge
                            (see Figure 6-7). The mathematical representation of the RWG basis is rather simple
                            and given by

                            origin at the nodes of the S +/− triangle opposite to the common edge, respectively.
                            Clearly, jn (r) vanishes to zero at the nodes opposite to the edge as r+/− have their
                            origin there. Also, its amplitude at the edge is maximum and equal to unity.

                            is nonzero only on a single pair of triangles. As such, the current density on each
                            triangle is a superposition of 3 weighted RWG basis (contributed by the three edges

             For m =  n, the evaluation of (6.18) to (6.21) can be done using a suitable
        numerical quadrature. We may, for example, use a seven-point quadrature as defined
        in Figure 6-8 with the corresponding samples and weights given in Table 6-3. This
        seven-point rule provides O(h 6 ) accuracy, where h is the radius of the circumscribing
        circle (Abramowitz and Stegun, 1972) with its tips lying on the circle: the (xi , yi )
        points in Figure 6-8 are referred to the origin of that circle. Also, when m = n,
        integrand singularities need to be carefully addressed. This will be discussed later
        in more detail.
             Direct and iterative solvers discussed in Section 6.3.8 and in Chapter 4 can be
        employed to solve the matrix system (6.12).
             The fidelity of the geometrical representation has direct impact on the solution
        of J via (6.12). At a minimum, it is important to make triangles (forming the mesh)
        small enough so that the rendered geometrical and electrical fidelity is maintained.
        Typically, the edge length of the triangles need be less than λ0 /10, where λ0 is the
        free-space wavelength at the solution frequency. The uniformity of the RWG (deter-
        mined by the uniformity of the mesh) is important in generating a well-conditioned
        matrix system. However, the density and size of the triangular elements may be
        constrained by the geometrical detail of the structure. In such cases, the mesh may
        contain very small elements in localized regions, often leading to ill-conditioned
        matrices. This is in part due to the so-called low-frequency breakdown of the EFIE

                         gral equations using triangular elements with RWG basis functions. Although trian-
                         gular elements are often sufficient for modeling 3-D geometries, geometrical errors
                         are introduced, particularly for curved surfaces. As can be realized, surface represen-
                         tations using flat facets introduce sharp wedges at their joints that are not in the orig-
                         inal geometry (see Figure 6-2). To minimize such geometrical and solution errors,
Volakis-7200025   book     ISBN : 9781891121937       October 5, 2011    14:31    271




                                     6.2      Curved Triangular and Quadrilateral Elements        271

        higher-order curvilinear elements were introduced (particularly in modeling airframe
        fine details). These higher-order elements also lead to fewer unknowns as there is no
        need to overdiscretize the geometry. The following section examines popular curvi-
        linear elements and their geometrical framework using curvilinear coordinates.


           6.2 CURVED TRIANGULAR AND
        QUADRILATERAL ELEMENTS
        Due to their mathematical simplicity and availability of related (commercial) mesh
        generation software, flat surface triangulations is a first choice in computational
        electromagnetic modeling (CEM). However, flat triangles have several shortcom-
        ings in modeling highly curved structures. Coarse meshes fail to capture geometry
        features, leading to inaccurate MoM solutions. An immediate remedy is to increase
        the density of the triangulation around the curved regions; however, this leads to an
        unnecessarily large number of unknowns in the MoM system since the number of
        basis functions is proportional to the total number of triangular elements in the mesh.
        More importantly, matrix conditioning deteriorates significantly as the triangulation
        is highly nonuniform, consisting on regions with very large and very small elements
        in proximity.
             An alternative to using facets to represent curved surfaces is to use curvilinear
        elements (triangular or quadrilateral). In this section, we develop the geometrical
        representation of several curvilinear elements. Conformal basis functions are also
        defined on these curved elements as tangential vector fields. Using curvilinear el-
        ements, we expect that high-fidelity geometry details of real-life structures will be
        mathematically represented without the need to increase mesh density (or the MoM
        matrix size). We first proceed with parametric representations of curves, surfaces,
        and volumes, providing concise definitions of line, surface, and volume elements as
        well as vector fields defined over these elements.

        6.2.1 Parametric Representations
        A space curve in 3-D can be represented as a mapping that transforms a unit element
        (e.g., a line of unit length) in the parameter space onto an arbitrary position vector
        in the (x, y, z). Such a representation is simply written as

                                           r(x, y, z) = r(u)                            (6.22)

        with the condition u ∈ [0, 1]. Several such parametric representations are shown in
        Figure 6-9. Typically, surface and volume mappings are constructed by a Cartesian
        product of one-dimensional transformations. For example, a curvilinear quadrilateral
        element in the (x, y, z) space can be constructed as the image of a unit square in the
        (u, v) space through the relation

                                             r = r(u, v)                                (6.23)

        where again u ∈ [0, 1] and v ∈ [0, 1]. Several typical curvilinear elements are shown
        in Figure 6-10. As in the case of facets, the geometrical surfaces can now be repre-
        sented as a mesh of curvilinear elements (see Figure 6-11).

        polynomials to represent arbitrary geometries can lead to restrictive geometrical

        in practice, polynomial interpolations are rarely used with higher-order polynomials.
             Alternatively, free-form representations, such as Bézier, B-spline, and nonuni-
        form rational B-splines (NURBS), are more widely used in manufacturing industry
        due to their flexibility and their unique representation properties; the following sec-
        tion provides a discussion.

        6.2.3 Free-Form Representations
        As already noted, interpolation meshes are constructed by constraining the surface
        elements to pass through predefined data points on the original surfac; that is, they
        are surface-fitting techniques. These methods are suitable surface approximations
        when a set of sampled data on the surface is available. However, when the surface
        body design also depends on functional and aesthetic requirements (e.g., the body of
        a custom designed automobile), one has to resort to a combination of computational
        and heuristic methods to mathematically represent the geometry. Bézier and B-spline
        curves and their rational counterparts (see, e.g., Farin, 1997) were developed with
        this goal in mind and are the backbone of mathematical models in computer-aided
        design (CAD) tools. In essence, these representations allow us to define both the
        points traversed by the curve and also the derivatives of the curve at that point. As
        such, continuity can be enforced at the interpolation points. The following sections
        discuss these tools, as they are becoming more widely used in CEM geometry
        representations as well.

        6.2.3.1 Bézier and B-Spline Curves and Surfaces
        A Bézier curve is specified by a set of points associated with a defining polygon. As
        such, the shape of the actual curve closely follows the shape of the defining polygon.
        For example, Figure 6-14 shows a generic third-order Bézier curve and its defining
        polygon.
            The Bézier curves have the following properties that make them particularly
        popular for generating and representing artistic designs:
        • The degree of the polynomial defining the curve segment is one less than the
          number of defining polygon points (this also holds for interpolation polynomials).

                         • The curve follows the shape of the defining polygon.
                         • The first and last points on the curve are coincident with the first and last points
                           of the defining polygon.
                         • The tangent vectors at the ends of the curve have the same direction as the first
                           and last polygon sides, respectively. These tangent vectors can be controlled by
                           changing the polygon points r2 and r3 .
                         • The curve is contained within the convex hull of the defining polygon, that is,
                           within the largest convex polygon obtainable with the defining polygon vertices.
                         • The curve exhibits the variation-diminishing property. This means that the curve
                           does not oscillate about a straight line more than the defining polygon.
                         • The curve is invariant under an affine transformation (a combination of linear
                           transformations such as translation and rotation).

                         several Bézier curves together. An nth degree B-spline curve is formed by connecting
                         nth degree Bézier curves and imposing (n −1)th derivative continuity at the junction
                         points. The local parameter of each Bézier curve runs from 0 to 1. A knot vector that
                         joins each Bézier polygon must also be prespecified. If this knot vector is nonuniform
                         then the resulting curve is called a nonuniform B-spline.

                              Unlike Bézier curves, B-splines have the desired property of local control; that
                         is, when one of its vertices is moved to a new location only the part of the curve
                         around that vertex changes. This is not the case for Bézier curves since the basis
                         functions Bin (u) are global (i.e., nonzero over the whole interval 0 ≤ u ≤ 1). Hence,
                         a change in the position of a single vertex affects the entire curve.
                              Rational extensions of Bézier and B-spline curves are appropriately named as
                         rational Bézier and rational B-spline curves. They allow one to assign additional

                             Cartesian-product B-spline surfaces are the natural extensions of Cartesian-product
                             Bézier surfaces, defined by

                             where Nim (u) and Njn (v) are the B-spline basis functions in the biparametric u
                             and v directions, respectively. These are blended Bézier surfaces used to transform a
                             B-spline surface to a set of connected Bézier surfaces (Farin, 1997). As with B-spline
                             curves, the shape and character of a B-spline surface is significantly influenced by
                             the knot vectors. Open, periodic, and nonuniform knot vectors are frequently used
                             in practice. For example, it is possible to use an open knot vector for one parametric
                             direction and a periodic knot vector for the other. This leads to a cylindrical surface
                             of varying cross sectional area. The local control properties of the B-spline curves
                             also carry over to B-spline surfaces.

        It should be noted that these surfaces are not tensor product surfaces themselves.
        Like their nonrational counterparts, open uniform, periodic uniform, and nonuniform
        knot vectors can be used to represent various rational Bézier and B-spline surfaces.
             In closing our discussion of free-form surface representations, we should note
        that a strong attraction of rational B-spline surfaces is their ability to represent
        quadric surfaces in 3-D. The general expression for quadric surfaces is given by

            Ax 2 + By 2 + C z 2 + Dx y + E yz + F x z + Gx + H y + J z + K = 0.         (6.42)

        NURBS surfaces can represent all such quadrics and blend them into higher-order
        sculptured surfaces. For example, one can represent a sphere exactly using a single
        rational B-spline surface as a collection of smoothly blended rational Bézier patches.
        The sphere and defining polygon net are shown in Figure 6-16.

            We remark that the triplet of vectors (au , av , n̂) forms a local conformal reference
        frame (at each surface point). It is assumed that no two such vectors are colinear (the
        surface is called “degenerate” if au and av are colinear).
            Typically, the vector functions F(r) = F(u, v) defined on a parametric surface
        r(u, v) can be represented in this coordinate frame as

                          F(u, v) = F (u) (u, v)au (u, v) + F (v) (u, v)av (u, v)          (6.46)

        where F (u) (u, v) and F (v) (u, v) are the contravariant components of the vector
        F(u, v). The basis vectors au (u, v) and av (u, v) are correspondingly called covariant
        vectors and form one of the two complementary basis in expressing the vector
        function F(u, v) on r(u, v). This representation can be extended to vector fields as
        outlined in Section 6.3 and are particularly useful in formulating and implementing
        conformal MoM solutions. Most subsequent implementations in this book are based
        on such parametric representations.
             A typical mesh of a geometry constructed using curvilinear elements (quadri-
        laterals) is shown in Figure 6-19. As indicated, conformal elements result in higher
        fidelity in geometrical representation including finer details that would otherwise
        require a much denser grid. As a result, curvilinear elements reduce the overall
        unknown count, leading to less memory and central processing unit (CPU) time.
        Indeed, the modeling fidelity, accuracy, and efficiency of MoM solutions using these
        elements have been reported in the literature from the 1990s on (Jin, Volakis, and

                         6.2.5.1 Parametric Representation of Volume Elements
                         Tetrahedral and prismatic elements are alternatives to hexahedral volume elements.
                         These can be considered as straightforward extensions of flat triangular elements and
                         are traditionally expressed in terms of barycentric coordinates. That is, any point
                         within a tetrahedron (defined by four distinct and non-colinear vertices r1 , r2 , r3 ,
                         and r4 ) can be obtained using its barycentric coordinates (ζ1 , ζ2 , ζ3 , ζ4 ) as
                                                                       

                         volumes of the subtetrahedral domains constructed by connecting the point r(ζ ) to
                         the vertices as shown in Figure 6-21a. That is, ζi = V jk /V . Using a similar logic, it
                         is possible to define curvilinear extensions of these tetrahedral elements, as shown
                         in Figure 6-21b. We direct the reader to Graglia (1987, 1988) and Graglia, Wilton,
                         and Peterson (1997) for a more detailed discussion on curvilinear tetrahedra.

        6.2.6 Example Representations of Surface and

        In this section, we provide the reader with explicit definition of the conformal basis

        for the (RWG) BFs on flat triangular elements. Subsequently, we introduce their
        curved counterparts defined on curved parametric surfaces described above.

             The vector field representing the basis function associated with the common
        edge of the quadrilateral pair is shown in Figure 6-29b. This BF consists of two half
        BFs (half BF 2 on element 1 and half BF 3 on element 2). Properly pairing these half-
        rooftop BFs on neighboring patches allows for a continuous current representation on
        the entire body. As required, the normal component of the current across neighboring
        patches is continuous; that is, no artificial charge accumulation exists on the common
        edge joining the pair of elements. More general higher-order basis functions can, of
        course, be constructed if the linear variations in (6.78) are replaced by higher-order
        functions. However, the accuracy of such representations should be correlated to
        the accuracy of the actual geometry model. That is, one should not pursue a higher-
        order representation of the current density aiming to improve solution accuracy if
        the geometry representation is not equally accurate. We do remark, however, that
        higher-order have been reported to generate smaller MoM systems. Hence, they
        can be advantageous as they may require less computational resources for the same
        accuracy solutions (Jorgensen, Volakis, Meincke, and Breinbjerg, 2004).

                         6.3.1 Element Matrices and Assembly Process
                         The double surface integrals in the matrix element expression (6.13) need to be
                         numerically evaluated to construct the MoM matrix using a suitable quadrature
                         rule. Since each basis and testing function is defined on a pair of elements, it is
                         advantageous to compute the contributions to the matrix entries from pairs of basis
                         and testing domains (i.e., compute element submatrices).
                              These contributions can be subsequently added into the actual matrix using the
                         mesh connectivity, as also done in standard finite element methods. Specifically, the
                         MoM matrix entries can be assembled as a combination of the 4 × 4 matrix elements
                         noted in Figure 6-30. Each of these takes the form

        self-cell evaluation has been a focus in many journal papers. Indeed, several integral
        evaluation techniques based on singularity extraction of flat elements were presented
        in Wilton, Rao, Glisson, Schaubert, Al-Bundak, and Butler (1984) and Eibert and
        Hansen (1996). However, these are not readily applicable to curvilinear elements.
        The following section explores singularity annihilation techniques for curvilinear el-
        ements. These are sufficiently general to be equally applicable for flat patches as well.

        element, respectively). This is an integrable singularity, but nevertheless it must be
        carefully evaluated numerically. In the next section, we present several annihilation

        is particularly important when n = m (i.e., for the MoM matrix self-terms). After

             The MoM matrix elements appearing in the formulations as double surface
        integrals on testing and basis subdomains are evaluated numerically differently de-
        pending on the distance between the testing and the basis functions. Generally,
        fixed-order Gaussian quadrature (Abramowitz and Stegun, 1972) is adapted for the
        evaluation of all MoM matrix integrals that do not involve overlapping of the inte-

        more careful consideration, as discussed next.

                         6.3.3 Singularity Annihilation Techniques

                         Eibert and Hansen, 1996). For our case, this approach works well for flat (faceted)

        6.3.5 Annihilation Transforms for Square Subdomains
        Referring to Figure 6-17, we recall that any curvilinear quadrilateral can be trans-

                         6.3.6 Numerical Integration
                         Other variations of the aforementioned techniques to annihilate the singularity of
                         the Green’s function on curved subdomains are, of course, possible (Duffy, 1982;
                         Graglia, 1987; Khayat and Wilton, 2005). From experience, it can be stated that for
                         triangular subdomains Method I performs best. Method I for quadrilateral subdo-
                         mains also performs best as it requires the least amount of computational resources.
                              Upon reaching a nonsingular integral using any of the methods presented in
                         Subsections 6.3.3–6.3.5, a fixed point Gaussian quadrature integration is acceptable
                         to evaluate the resulting integrals. Of course, greater accuracy can be achieved by
                         increasing the integration order.
                              Once the matrix elements are computed, the resulting matrix system must be
                         solved to determine the unknown column {xi } for i = 1, 2, . . . , N . A direct solu-
                         tion method, such as Gaussian elimination or lower-upper (LU) decomposition can
                         always be used to solve for {xi }. However, the computational resources required
                         by a direct solver are very high (O(N 3 )) as was noted in Chapter 4. As iterative
                         algorithms (Saad, 1996; Topsakal, Kindt, Sertel, and Volakis, 2001) have O(N 2 )
                         complexity (per iteration), they are much more attractive for matrix systems where
                         N can reach several millions of unknowns. The hope with iterative methods is to
                         achieve convergence in few iterations. Several preconditioning methods can be em-
                         ployed to achieve quick convergence (Sertel and Volakis, 2000). In addition, the fast
                         multipole method (FMM) (Coifman, Rokhlin, and Wandzura, 1993) and the adaptive
                         integral method (AIM) (Bleszynski, Bleszynski, and Jaroszewicz, 1996) are ways
                         to speed up the matrix-vector products executed in any iterative solver. These are
                         examined in Chapter 7.

                         6.3.8 Matrix Solution Methods
                          So far, we have discussed the MoM procedure to convert integral representations
                         into a linear system of equations. The governing integro-differential equations were
                         discretized concurrently representing the solution space as a discrete mesh of con-
                         nected finite elements with the unknowns as a summation of weighted basis func-
                         tions. This is the most common method for solving problems involving arbitrary
                         geometries. Other MoM discretizations using entire domain basis functions, have
                         also been employed (Popović and Kolundžija, 1994; Notaros and Popovic, 1996;
                         Notaros, Popovic, Weem, Brown, and Popovic, 2001). However, these require some
                         level of a priori knowledge of the field behavior. Although simpler specialized dis-
                         cretizations, such as mode matching or entire domain bases, result in much smaller
                         systems, the applicability of such MoM implementations are rather limited.
                              Typically, when the size of the matrix system is less that a few thousand, the
                         system is solved via a direct method, such as LU decomposition as discussed in
                         Chapter 4 (Section 4.3). Alternatively, for larger problems iterative solvers provide
                         a much faster solution that direct solvers (see Section 4.11). For large problems,
                         fast and efficient methods that minimize storage of the matrix system are necessary
                         as well. The fast methods will be discussed in Chapter 7 and they rely on iterative
                         solvers as they are based on accelerating the matrix-vector products.
                              Direct and iterative algorithms were mentioned in Chapter 4. Next, we discuss
                         possible preconditioners. These are critically needed in the iterative solvers. They
                         are particularly essential for not well-conditioned matrix systems.

                         6.3.8.1 Preconditioning Approaches
                         For large-scale simulations (possibly with geometrical surface details, e.g., antenna
                         arrays on aircraft), the density of the surface mesh is likely to be highly nonuniform.
                         Nonuniform meshes are known to produce ill-conditioned MoM matrix equations.
                         Such meshes are rather typical in most realistic antenna and scattering problems.
                         Therefore, use of preconditioners to lower the matrix condition number is essential.
                              The diagonal preconditioner is simple and leads to significant convergence
                         improvements. However, it does so only for diagonally dominant matrices. On the
                         other hand, block diagonal preconditioners are more robust but require renumbering
                         of the mesh or matrix rearranging so that the dominant matrix terms are clustered
                         around the diagonal. This can be done more readily for 2-D problems but is quite
                         difficult in 3-D. Alternatively, with iterative solvers, sparse matrix preconditioners
                         can be used instead of block preconditioners.
Volakis-7200025    book     ISBN : 9781891121937               October 5, 2011   14:31    311




                                                         6.3       Evaluation of MoM Matrix Entries        311

             A simple way to generate an effective preconditioning matrix is to execute an
        LU decomposition on the near-field (near-diagonal band) matrix. Depending on the
        sparsity of the near-field matrix, this LU process may require a significant CPU
        time. Thus, for large matrix systems this is not an attractive approach. Next, we
        mention some popular preconditioning approaches. To avoid the large CPU times
        in generating the preconditioner, we can instead employ an incomplete LU (ILU)
        factorization of the matrix (Saad, 1996). The ILU algorithm is identical to a direct
        LU algorithm, but it avoids fill-ins of elements in the decomposed LU matrices.
        Thus, much less CPU time is required. The ILU (and its variants) can be found
        in (Saad, 1996). A pseudo code is repeated herein for completeness:
                  for i = 2,...,n, do:
                    for k = 1,...,i-1 and for (i,k) in NZ(Z) do:
                       compute zik = zik /zkk
                       for j = k+1,...,n and for (i,j) in NZ(Z) do:
                         compute zij = zij − zik zkj
                       end do
                    end do
                  end do
        Here NZ(Z) is the sparsity pattern of the near-field matrix [Z]. As the conventional
        LU decomposition algorithm is applied only to the nonzero entries of the matrix,
        the memory is not affected, and the sparsity pattern of the stored ILU matrix is the
        same as the original one.
             Recently, approximate inverse preconditioners based on direct inversion of sub-
        sections of the MoM matrix were proposed. Their implementation details and per-
        formance evaluations can be found in (Carr, Bleszynski, and Volakis, 2004).

        computed during the MoM matrix computation phase of the solver. However, the
        generation of the dual complex and the associated BC basis functions requires careful
        bookkeeping of the various indices involved. Nonetheless, the computational sav-
        ings of the Calderon preconditioner, in particular for low-frequency problems, were
        reported in Andriulli, Cools, Bagci, Olyslager, Buffa, Christiansen, and Michielssen
        (2008). Furthermore, a loop-star basis function version is given in Stephanson and
        Lee (2009) showing both improved convergence and immunity to low-frequency
        breakdown.


        6.3.9 Performance of Preconditioned Conjugate
        Gradient Squared Solver
        For example, to evaluate the performance of the popular ILU preconditioner, we
        considered the scattering by the PEC ogive depicted in Figure 6-47. The ILU pre-
        conditioner was implemented using all three formulations (EFIE, MFIE, and CFIE).
        As we already noted, the CFIE converged much faster due to its better conditioning.
        Thus, preconditioning of the CFIE may not have much of an effect in solution time.
        The size of the matrix system was N = 480 and refers to a 10 long ×2 diameter
        ogive (with its long axis coincident with the x-axis). All calculations were carried
        out at 5.91 GHz.
            Figure 6-48 shows the residual error as a function of iteration number for the
        EFIE matrix. It is seen that due to the irregular mesh around the sharp tips, the
        conjugate gradient squared (CGS) solver does not show tendency for convergence
        even after 50 iterations. However, once the ILU preconditioner is employed, con-
        vergence is dramatically improved, requiring only N/50 iterations (N = number of
        unknowns) to achieve a residual error of 10−5 (Section 4.11).
            Nonpreconditioned and preconditioned solution data for the MFIE matrix are
        given in Figure 6-49. Since the MFIE formulation always leads to better conditioned
        systems (this is apart from its formulation accuracy), residual error shows some
        tendency for convergence. Regardless, convergence without preconditioning is very

                  6.4      VOLUMETRIC MODELING
        Volume integral equation formulations were discussed in Chapter 3 at some length
        (Peterson, 1991; Arvas, Rahhal-Arabi, and Sadigh, 1991; Volakis, 1992). Here, we
        revisit these formulations and present MoM solutions.
             Indeed, with the recent success of fast integral methods, such as the
        multilevel FMM (MLFMM) (Coifman, Rokhlin, and Wandzura, 1993; Chew, Jin,
        Lu, Michielssen, and Song, 1997), it is important to reexamine VIE methods refering
        to Section 3.1.7 in modeling inhomogeneous volumetric structures (Lu, 2001). In this
        chapter, we develop a VIE solution method using curvilinear hexahedral elements
        for penetrable structures. We introduce the MLFMM formulation for the pertinent
        VIEs in Chapter 7, Section 7.5. It is demonstrated that even piecewise constant basis
        functions provide excellent accuracy at a nominal sampling rates when conformal
        elements are used.

        Numerical evaluation of these matrix elements can again be carried out using a

        the self-cell interactions is treated separately using an annihilation technique similar
        to that used for SIEs (Sertel and Volakis, 2002).
             In the next section, we summarize several different orders of volumetric basis
        functions to be used in (6.184). In particular, we describe three different orders of
        basis functions, each having specific qualities attractive for volumetric modeling.
        For purely dielectric bodies, all three basis functions are observed to generate ac-
        curate results. However, when the target geometry has nontrivial permittivity and
        permeability, as discussed in the next section, second-order basis functions must be
        due to the need to carry out the differentiation in ∇ × E appearing in (6.179).

        6.4.3 Zeroth-Order Volumetric Basis Functions
        For each curvilinear hexahedral volume element shown in Figure 6-52, three basis
        functions associated with the three parametric directions can be defined as

        It is easy to show that the divergence of the previous basis function (inside the
        element) is identically zero. This is a property shared by the electric field inside
        a uniform dielectric region. Thus, it is an important property to maintain. Another
        advantage of this expansion is that the basis functions are defined on separate ele-
        ments. Hence, this expansion allows for a natural decomposition of the problem into
        different domains. It is important to note that the normal components of the basis
        functions are allowed to be discontinuous. We remark that these basis functions are

        6.4.6 Scattering by Dielectric Bodies
        In this section, we examine the three previously outlined volumetric basis func-
        tions to compute the scattering from a dielectric shell. Figure 6-55 depicts the com-
        puted bistatic RCS curves for a dielectric shell of outer radius 0.2λ0 and thickness
        0.02λ0 . As seen, all three results agree well with the analytical solution. We note that
        although the same volume mesh is used in all three cases, the system sizes for
        different basis functions are inherently different. For this specific example, zeroth-
        order basis functions resulted in 648 unknowns, the first-order basis functions led to
        864 unknowns, and the second-order basis functions resulted in 1, 082 unknowns.
        Correspondingly, the matrix fill times were different, with the zeroth order being the
        fastest and the second order being the slowest.

        Figure 6-59). The incident plane wave is propagating in the negative z-direction,

                        √

        good for both polarizations.
             As a second example, we again consider a thin spherical shell having outer radius
        of 0.2λ0 , thickness 0.02λ0 , and the same material parameters (r = 1.5, μr = 2.2)
        as in the previous example. For modeling, the mesh is constructed entirely as a thin
        layer of distorted (nonrectangular) curvilinear elements, and both the VIE and FE-BI
        solution used the same mesh. The bistatic RCS is shown in Figure 6-60, and it is
        clear that the solutions are again in full agreement.
             As our third example, we evaluate the RCS of a solid sphere of radius 0.15λ0 .
        The permittivity and permeability of the sphere are again r = 1.5 and μr = 2.2,
        respectively. We used the same volumetric mesh as shown in Figure 6-61 for both
        the VIE and FE-BI methods. Again, excellent agreement is seen between the VIE
        and FE-BI solutions.
             We close this section by noting that, in contrast to the SIE, the VIE is a second
        kind integral equation, and its iterative solution converges quickly. As an example,
        for a system of 1082 VIE unknowns (second example), the CGS solver converged
        in five iterations for a relative error of 10−2 . Also the overall solution was com-
        pleted in only 0.7 seconds using a 1 GHz PIII processor. For the third example
        (880 VIE unknowns), the iterative CGS solver converged in 13 iterations and took
        1.1 seconds.

                          6.4.7.1 Volume-Surface Integral Equations
                          When the problem geometry involves multiple material regions embedded in a high-
                          contrast background, it may be more attractive to modify the VIE formulations
                          previously given to reduce its high computational cost of discretizing the high-
                          contrast background. An alternative is the VSIE described in detail in Volakis, Sertel,
                          and Usner (2006). In particular, the VSIE formulation is very attractive for high-
                          contrast materials that have slight variations in their permittivity or permeabilities.
                              Considering the geometry shown in Figure 6-62, the VSIE formulation relies
                          on the following factorization of the material permittivity

                                                               r (r) = b I +  δ (r) = b [I + b−1  δ (r)] = b   (r).         (6.196)

                          Similarly, the permeability μr is written as

                                                                      b μδ (r)] = μb μ (r).                                         (6.197)

                              Notice that (6.199) involves three electromagnetic quantities as unknowns,
                         namely, the electric fields Ei within each domain Vi , and the surface currents J̃i , and
                         Mi over the boundaries Si of each subdomain. Hence, three equations are needed
                         to solve for these three unknowns, the first of which is given in (6.199) as a mixed
                         volume-surface integral enforced over each subdomain Vi . The second equation re-

                                 6.5        SCATTERING EXAMPLES
                         To demonstrate the presented moment method techniques, in this section we consider
                         several radar scattering examples. Surface meshes of the related test geometries
                         (using curvilinear quadrilaterals) are given in Figure 6-63.
                              In each of these meshes, the density is such that the edge length is maintained
                         around λ0 /10 (λ0 being the free-space wavelength at the simulation frequency).
                         The commercially available meshing package PATRAN (MSC Software, 2010) was
                         used to generate these surface meshes. We note that the meshes in Figure 6-63a,
                         6-63c and 6-63e are of the paver type and Figure 6-64 compares such a mesh to an
                         isoparametric one. As depicted, the isoparametric mesh in Figure 6-64a generates
                         more uniform structured meshes. However, depending on the curvature of the surface
                         being gridded, some of the element may be severely distorted leading to ill-
                         conditioned matrices. In contrast, the paver mesh (such as the one shown in
                         Figure 6-64b) is rid of extreme distortions within the mesh. Next, we provide nu-
                         merical results using both kinds of meshes for the same geometry and demonstrate
                         that each mesh provide comparable accuracy.

             The first test geometry being considered is a PEC sphere of radius 1 m, depicted
        in Figure 6-63a. This is a unique 3-D geometry that lends itself to an analytical
        solution (Mie series) for its radar scattering. Hence, a reference solution is available
        for evaluating the numerical solution accuracy.
             Figure 6-65 compares the bistatic RCS for this 1 m radius sphere at 300 MHz
        using the paver and isoparametric meshes for both E- and H-polarizations. Clearly,
